# Sprint 2 Individual Reflection

**Student:** Ethan Kidd  
**Course:** CS 3660 Web Design 2, Summer 2026  
**Sprint:** Sprint 2 — Fleet Monitor  
**Date:** June 2026

---

## What I built

This sprint I built a distributed fleet telemetry system from scratch. The core idea is that simulated vehicles publish raw sensor readings over MQTT, a gateway pipeline cleans and enriches them, and an alert engine maintains a state machine for every monitored channel. A browser dashboard shows live fleet state and lets operators acknowledge and resolve alerts.

The system covers six monitored channels across three vehicles: coolant temperature, oil pressure, RPM, and fuel level. Each channel gets its own XState v5 machine instance with six states (NORMAL, WARNING, CRITICAL, ACKNOWLEDGED, RESOLVED, OFFLINE) and hysteresis so a single noisy reading cannot flip the state.

What I am most proud of is the append-only event store. Every domain event is written to a SHA-256 hash-chained SQLite table. Because nothing is ever updated or deleted, you can select all events up to any timestamp, fold them through the pure reducer, and recover the exact fleet state at that moment in history. The time-travel slider in the dashboard uses this directly.

---

## Patterns I applied

**Publish-Subscribe Channel (EIP)** was the backbone. Every component is decoupled: the device simulator does not know the gateway exists, the gateway does not know the alert engine exists, and so on. Each process just subscribes to the topics it cares about. This made it possible to add the audit-logger and ws-bridge later without touching any existing code.

**Message Translator, Message Router, and Content Enricher (EIPs)** form a pipeline in the gateway. The translator normalizes and validates raw sensor payloads. The router resolves the output topic from the message content without modifying the message. The enricher adds vehicle metadata, thresholds, and a rolling average so every downstream consumer receives a self-describing message and does not need its own lookup tables. Keeping these as three separate classes instead of one big function made them independently testable and easy to reason about.

**Strategy (GoF)** in the alert engine lets me swap the comparison logic per metric without touching the state machine. RateOfChangeStrategy fires when the per-reading delta is too large, which matters for RPM spikes even when the absolute value is fine. Having a StrategyFactory that selects the right strategy at runtime kept the machine itself clean.

**Observer (GoF)** in the event system was the cleanest pattern of the sprint. The EventDispatcher does not know whether AuditLogger or WsBridgeObserver exist. I just register them at startup. When a domain event fires, both run. This means the audit trail and the live dashboard update are completely decoupled from the alert engine logic that produced the event.

## What was hard

The hardest debugging session was the blank dashboard. All four processes were running, MQTT subscriptions were confirmed, and the gateway was visibly publishing to clean topics, but the alert engine showed no output and the dashboard never populated. It turned out that `clean: false` with stable client IDs on a shared public broker (test.mosquitto.org) caused the broker to hold stale session state from earlier development machines. When a new alert-engine session connected with the same client ID, the broker handed it a backlog of expired session data instead of forwarding live messages. The fix was `clean: true` plus a `Date.now()` suffix on client IDs during development. The root cause was subtle because everything looked healthy from the outside.

The event store hash chain was also tricky to get right. SHA-256 of `(prev_hash + canonical(payload))` sounds simple, but getting `canonical` to be deterministic required sorting object keys before serializing. A non-deterministic hash would break chain verification silently.

---

## What I would do differently

I would set up the dashboard and ws-bridge earlier. I left them until Week 3 and spent the first two weeks testing the pipeline entirely with terminal output and inject scripts. Having a visual while building the alert machine would have caught the stale-session bug and the hysteresis edge cases much faster.

I would also write the integration test first, before any other code. The test that publishes a raw reading and asserts an alert event appears in the event store forced me to get the full pipeline wired correctly. Writing it last meant I found the wiring issues at the end instead of the beginning.

---

## What I learned

XState v5 is a significant departure from v4. The `createMachine` / `createActor` API and the way guards and actions are defined as plain objects in the config rather than as string references took real adjustment. Once it clicked, the state machine approach is genuinely better than the if/else chains I would have written otherwise. The machine is self-documenting: the state chart table in the README is derived directly from the machine definition.

I also learned that append-only event stores are not a theoretical concept. Building point-in-time reconstruction with a real slider in a real browser made it concrete. The reducer fold is a few lines of code, but the implications for auditability are significant.

The EIP patterns from the Gateway of Eden are more useful than they looked in lecture. Naming things Translator, Router, and Enricher forced clarity about what each piece actually does and stopped me from writing one god-function that did all three.

---

## Hours

Approximately 40 hours across four weeks, spread across design, implementation, debugging, and testing.
